lesson_title: The Bakkie and the Bag of Ore: Industrial and Regional Development
hook_text: South Africa sells a bag of iron ore for a few hundred rand — then buys it back as machinery for a fortune. Here's the plan to stop that.
clip_script: Two exports on the same dock. A bag of iron ore: a few hundred rand, plus the wages of the digging. A bakkie: hundreds of thousands of rand — and inside that price sit the steelworker's wages, the component maker's, the assembler's, the painter's, plus every firm's profits and taxes along the way. Same iron. The country that does the MAKING gets rich. That's value added — and doing it before export is called beneficiation. And a factory never stands alone: behind the plant, tyre makers, glass makers, transporters; in front of it, dealers and mechanics. Hundreds of businesses off one assembly line. So government leans on the scale. Carmakers earn rewards for building here — that's why seven global brands assemble in South Africa. Coega got a deep-water port, a ready-built zone, and a 15 percent tax rate for factories that move in. The N4 to Maputo woke up a whole line of towns. But history keeps one warning lit: apartheid paid factories to move to the homelands — and when the subsidies stopped, the factories died. You can pay a factory to arrive anywhere. It only stays where the lights stay on, the trains run, and the business actually works.
visual_style: A split dock scene — a shrinking bag of ore against a growing bakkie assembled piece by piece; a web of supplier icons lighting up around one factory; a map of South Africa with zones and the N4 corridor glowing, then one homeland factory flickering out.
mood: Ambitious and clear-eyed, national-project energy with an honest edge.
pacing: Slow weigh-in on the two exports, quickening through the linkage web and the named zones, a deliberate beat on the homeland warning.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and judge South Africa's industrial strategy like a marker — wins, failures and the real bottleneck.
